summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 works with the revised IPsec architecture and IKEv2. It updates how the security associations that protect mobility signaling are set up and used. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device roams away from its home network, it keeps a home address and tells its home router about the new address it is using. These messages need protection. This RFC describes how to protect them with the current version of IPsec and with IKEv2, the protocol that sets up the protection, including the option to check the user's credentials against another server.

subtitle: How Mobile IPv6 signalling is protected with the revised IPsec architecture and IKEv2.

tldr.problem: RFC 3776 described how to protect Mobile IPv6 signalling with IPsec, but IPsec has since been rewritten and the key exchange protocol with it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC restates the requirements for mobile nodes and home agents under the revised IPsec architecture, where the mobility message type is a selector, and it describes how IKEv2 negotiates the security associations, including with EAP authentication.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 3776 and adds a way for a mobile node to receive its home address over IKEv2, with the address lifetime tied to the lifetime of the security association.

facts.label: New IPsec selectors
facts.value: Mobility Header message type, ICMPv6 message type and code

today: RFC 4877 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3776, replacing its use of the older IPsec architecture with the revised architecture in RFC 4301 and IKEv2 as specified in RFC 4306.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Earlier Specification
sections.content:
RFC 3776 describes how IPsec, as described in RFC 2401, is used with Mobile IPv6 to protect the signalling messages, and it illustrates examples of Security Policy Database and Security Association Database entries for that purpose. This RFC updates it.

The IPsec architecture has been revised in RFC 4301. Among the many changes, the list of selectors has been expanded to include the Mobility Header message type. That changes how security policies and security associations are configured for protecting mobility header messages: it becomes easier to differentiate between the various Mobility Header messages from the type value, instead of checking whether a particular mobility header message is being sent on a tunnel interface between the mobile node and the home agent, as was the case in RFC 3776. The revised architecture also includes the ICMP message type and code as selectors, which makes it possible to protect Mobile Prefix Discovery messages without applying the same security associations to all ICMPv6 messages.

The Internet Key Exchange protocol has also been substantially revised and simplified. This RFC discusses the new requirements for the home agent and the mobile node to use the revised IPsec architecture and IKEv2. Section 4 lists the requirements, and sections 6 and 7 describe the required Security Policy Database and Security Association Database entries for manual and dynamic configuration. The use of EAP within IKEv2 is allowed to authenticate the mobile node to the home agent, and a method for dynamically configuring a home address using the Configuration Payload in IKEv2 is described as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IPv6 needs the signalling messages between a roaming device and its home router to be protected. The earlier specification did that with the older version of IPsec. This RFC updates it to the revised IPsec architecture and to IKEv2, the newer key exchange protocol, and it sets out exactly what each device must configure.

sections.title: Packet Formats for Tunneled Signaling
sections.content:
The mobile node and the home agent MUST support the packet formats as defined in section 3 of RFC 3776.

In case the mobile node reverse tunnels all traffic, including the Mobile IPv6 signalling messages exchanged between the mobile node and the home agent, the Home Address Option is not required to be present in the messages sent to the home agent. The packet format for the binding update when sent in tunnel mode looks as follows.

IPv6 hdr (source = care-of address, destination = home agent)
ESP header in tunnel mode
IPv6 hdr (source = home address, destination = home agent)
Mobility Header
   Binding Update
      Alternate Care-of Address option (care-of address)

The binding acknowledgement sent to the mobile node when it is away from the home link looks as follows.

IPv6 hdr (source = home agent, destination = care-of address)
ESP header in tunnel mode
IPv6 hdr (source = home agent, destination = home address)
Mobility Header
   Binding Acknowledgement

The packet formats for tunneled mobile prefix discovery messages are very similar to the tunneled binding update and binding acknowledgement, with the home address as the source address in the inner IP header. Support for the tunneled packet format is optional on the mobile node and the home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Two copies of an IPv6 header wrap the protected message. The outer header carries the roaming address, so the traffic can cross the Internet, and the inner header carries the home address, so the receiver sees the address it expects.

sections.title: Requirements on the Mobile Node and Home Agent
sections.content:
Section 4 describes mandatory rules for all Mobile IPv6 mobile nodes and home agents, so that IPsec, with IKEv2 as the key management protocol, can protect traffic between the mobile node and the home agent. Many of the requirements are repeated from RFC 3776 to make the document self-contained.

The general requirements include that ESP encapsulation for Binding Updates and Binding Acknowledgements MUST be supported and used, and that ESP encapsulation in tunnel mode for the Home Test Init and Home Test messages tunneled between the mobile node and the home agent MUST be supported and SHOULD be used. ESP encapsulation of the ICMPv6 messages related to mobile prefix discovery MUST be supported and SHOULD be used, while ESP encapsulation of the payload packets tunneled between the two MAY be supported and used. If multicast group membership control protocols or stateful address autoconfiguration protocols are supported, payload data protection MUST be supported for those protocols.

The policy requirements say that, because the Mobility Header message type is now a selector, per-interface configuration of security policies is not required for protecting mobility header messages. The RFC notes the limit of that: without per-interface security policies, payload packet protection is limited to packets originating or terminating at the home address, and traffic using a link-local address within the Mobile IP tunnel cannot be given IPsec protection. The home agent MUST also be able to prevent a mobile node from using its security association to send a binding update on behalf of another mobile node, and it uses the Peer Authorization Database to store the per-mobile-node state that ties a mobile node's identity to its home address.

The IPsec processing requirements say that both devices SHOULD support the Mobility Header message type and the ICMPv6 message type as selectors, and that the home agent MUST be able to tell HoTi messages addressed to itself, when it is acting as a Correspondent Node, from those addressed to Correspondent Nodes, when it is acting as a home agent. When securing Binding Updates, Binding Acknowledgements and Mobile Prefix Discovery messages, both devices MUST support the ESP header in transport mode and MUST use a non-null payload authentication algorithm. The use of the ESP sequence number for anti-replay protection is optional, because the sequence numbers in the Binding Updates provide it, but that protection fails if the home agent loses its binding cache state, so complete anti-replay protection can only be provided by a dynamic keying mechanism such as IKEv2.

Because ESP leaves the care-of address in the outer IPv6 header unprotected, Mobile IPv6 implementations MUST use the Alternate Care-of Address option in Binding Updates sent while away from home, so that the home agent can verify that the address has not been tampered with. The dynamic keying requirements say that the mobile node MUST use its care-of address as source address in protocol exchanges when using dynamic keying, and that both devices MUST create security associations based on the home address, so that the associations survive changes in the care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists what each side must do. Binding updates and acknowledgements are protected with ESP in transport mode, return routability messages with ESP in tunnel mode, and prefix discovery messages are protected too. The protection is keyed on the home address, so it keeps working when the device moves to a new network.

sections.title: How Precisely the Traffic Is Selected
sections.content:
IPsec implementations are compatible with this document even if they do not support fine-grain selectors such as the Mobility Header message type and the ICMPv6 message type, although such implementations are not compliant with RFC 4301. For various reasons some implementations support only coarse-grain selectors, that is, addresses and in some cases the protocol field, for forwarded traffic. Because finer-grain selectors give better control, since the protection is applied only when it is required, the examples in the document always use the finest granularity.

The RFC describes three ways of setting up IPsec policies for Mobile IPv6 messages. In the first, the implementations on the mobile node and the home agent support fine-grain selectors including the Mobility Header message type, which is the case assumed in the examples. In the second, the implementations support selectors at protocol level only, so they can identify mobility header traffic but not the individual messages; the protection of Return Routability messages then uses a setup similar to the regular payload packets sent to the correspondent node, with the protocol selector set to Mobility Header, and all tunneled Mobility Header messages are protected. In the third, the protocol selector is not available at all, so all traffic sent by the mobile node that is reverse tunneled through the home agent is protected using ESP in tunnel mode, with the protocol selector set to any. That third case also applies when the mobile node tunnels all traffic to the home agent for privacy reasons.

The third case brings two extra considerations. If there is just one security association providing protection for all traffic, it MUST fulfil the requirements for protecting the Return Routability messages, which require confidentiality protection. Where the third case is used for privacy reasons, separate tunnel mode policy entries can protect the Return Routability messages with a higher priority, so that the entry with the higher priority is applied first. The second consideration is that the Binding Update which updates the tunnel endpoint arrives through the same tunnel that has to be updated, so the home agent has to be careful not to drop it, either by checking the source address on the outer IPv6 header after the binding update is processed or by exception handling that checks the inner packet when the outer source address does not match.
sections.plainLanguage: How well the protection can be aimed depends on the IPsec implementation. A device that understands the mobility message types can protect only the messages that need it. A simpler device protects everything in the tunnel instead, which is safer but uses more of the link's capacity.

sections.title: Negotiating Security Associations with IKEv2
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 signalling messages are typically initiated by the mobile node, which sends a Binding Update to the home agent whenever it moves and acquires a new care-of address. The mobile node initiates an IKEv2 exchange if the required security associations are not present.

A possible mechanism for mutual authentication is a shared secret between the mobile node and the home agent, and the home agent uses the identity of the mobile node to identify the corresponding shared secret. When a public-key-based mechanism is available, it should be the preferred mechanism. If a shared secret is used, the mobile node uses it to generate the AUTH payload in the IKE_AUTH exchange; if it uses a public-key-based mechanism, it uses its private key.

The exchange has four messages. The mobile node sends the first with its proposed security association, its key exchange payload and a nonce. The home agent replies with its own proposal, its key exchange payload, a nonce and, optionally, a certificate request. The mobile node then sends an encrypted message carrying its identity, optionally a certificate and a certificate request, the home agent's identity if it was learned, the AUTH payload, its second security association proposal and the traffic selectors. The home agent answers with an encrypted message carrying its identity, optionally a certificate, its AUTH payload, its second security association proposal and the traffic selectors.

The mobile node always includes its identity in the IDi payload in the IKE_AUTH exchange. It can identify itself with its statically configured home address, in which case the ID Type field is set to ID_IPV6_ADDR, with a Fully Qualified Domain Name, with the ID Type field set to ID_FQDN, or with an RFC 822 identifier, with the ID Type field set to ID_RFC822_ADDR. The list of identities is not exhaustive.

In the IKE_AUTH exchange the mobile node includes the home address and the appropriate selectors in the TSi payload, to negotiate the security associations that protect the Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgement messages. After IKE_AUTH completes, the mobile node initiates CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges to negotiate the additional associations for Return Routability signalling, Mobile Prefix Discovery messages and, optionally, payload traffic. Those exchanges are protected by the IKEv2 security associations created during the IKE_SA_INIT exchange.

It is important that the security associations are created based on the home address, so that they survive a change of care-of address, and the mobile node MUST use its home address as the initiator IP address in the TSi payload of the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. When public-key authentication is used, the identity in the IDi payload MUST correspond to the identity in the certificate the home agent obtains, and if the mobile node presents its home address the home agent MUST verify that the home address matches an iPAddress field in the SubjectAltName extension.
sections.plainLanguage: When the device needs new protected channels, it negotiates them with the home router using IKEv2. Both sides prove who they are with a shared secret or a certificate, and the mobile device asks for protection of the specific message types it needs.

sections.title: Using EAP to Authenticate the Mobile Node
sections.content:
In addition to using public key signatures and shared secrets, EAP can be used with IKEv2 for authenticating the mobile node to the home agent.

The mobile node indicates that it wants to use EAP by including the IDi payload but leaving out the AUTH payload in the first message during the IKE_AUTH exchange. The home agent then includes an EAP payload if it is willing to use an extensible authentication method. Security associations are not created until the subsequent IKE_AUTH exchange, after successful EAP authentication. The RFC notes that the use of EAP adds at least two round trips to the IKE negotiation, and that the number of round trips depends on the EAP method used.

When EAP is used, the identity the mobile node presents in the IDi field may not be its actual identity. It could be set to an identity used only for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting routing purposes and for selecting the right EAP method, and the actual identity may be carried inside EAP, invisible to the home agent. IKEv2 does not allow an EAP Identity Request or Response message exchange, but EAP methods may exchange identities within themselves. In that case the home agent MUST acquire the mobile node's identity from the corresponding AAA server, and how it does so is out of scope for this document.

Some EAP methods generate a shared key on the mobile node and the home agent once the EAP authentication succeeds. That shared key is used to generate the AUTH payloads in the subsequent IKEv2 messages, and it MUST NOT be used for any other purpose. The use of EAP between the mobile node and the home agent might also require the home agent to contact an authorization server such as the AAA Home server on the home link.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP lets the home router ask another system, such as a corporate login server, to check the user's credentials. It costs at least two extra round trips, and the real identity of the user may stay hidden inside the EAP exchange.

sections.title: Getting a Home Address over IKEv2
sections.content:
The mobile node can dynamically configure a home address by including a Configuration Payload in the IKE_AUTH exchange, with a request for an address from the home link. It should include a zero-length INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS attribute in the CFG_REQUEST payload, and it MAY include multiple instances of that attribute to request several home addresses.

When the home agent receives a configuration payload with a CFG_REQUEST for INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS, it replies with a valid home address for the mobile node. The INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS attribute in the CFG_REPLY contains the prefix length of the home prefix in addition to a 128 bit home address. The home agent could use a local database or contact a DHCPv6 server on the home link. The duration for which the home address is allocated is the same as the duration for which an IKEv2 security association exists between the mobile node and the home agent, and if that association is rekeyed, the home address lifetime is extended as well.

The mobile node could suggest a home address that it wants to use in the CFG_REQUEST, for example one allocated for it before or one it auto-configured from the IPv6 prefix on the home link. The home agent can let the mobile node keep the same address by setting the INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS attribute in the CFG_REPLY to that address, or send a new address if it wants a different one, in which case the mobile node MUST stop using its old home address and start using the newly allocated one.

If the home agent is unable to allocate a home address during the IKE_AUTH exchange, it MUST send a Notify payload with an INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE message, and the mobile node then SHOULD terminate the IKE_AUTH exchange, start a new IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH exchange and try to auto-configure a home address. It MAY also switch to another home agent, whose address can come from a home agent list received during an earlier discovery phase or, if that list is empty or not available, from a new discovery attempt. If the mobile node wants to configure a DNS server from the home link, it can request the DNS server information by including an INTERNAL_IP6_DNS attribute in the CFG_REQUEST payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The device can ask for its home address over the same secure channel it uses for everything else. The home router picks an address from its own records or from a DHCPv6 server, and the address is valid for as long as the secure channel lasts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC refers to RFC 3775 for the security considerations that apply to the use of IPsec with Mobile IPv6, and to RFC 4306 for those that apply to the use of EAP with IKEv2.

It adds one point of its own. A misbehaving mobile node could create IPsec security associations for a home address that belongs to another mobile node. The home agent should therefore check that a particular mobile node is authorized to use a home address before creating security associations for that home address. If the home address was assigned as described in section 9, the home agent MUST associate the home address with the identity used in the IKE negotiation, and it MAY store the assigned home address in the security policy entries created for the mobile node.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is one mobile device pretending to be another so that it can claim its home address. The home router therefore checks that the identity it authenticated is allowed to use the address before it sets up protection for it.

items.title: Fine-grain selectors
items.text: The implementation understands the mobility message type, so only the messages that need protection are protected.

items.title: Protocol-level selectors
items.text: The implementation sees only mobility header traffic, so all tunneled mobility header messages are protected together.

items.title: No protocol selector
items.text: Everything the mobile node tunnels through the home agent is protected with ESP in tunnel mode.
